criteria.description: Correctly matches (a) to CNN with spatial-structure reasoning.
Correctly matches (b) to LSTM/GRU with sequential-structure reasoning.
Correctly matches (c) to Transformer with permutation-invariance reasoning.

solutions.fullSolution: (a) CNN: photographs have spatial/grid structure; convolution's weight sharing exploits translation invariance. (b) LSTM/GRU: sequential/temporal structure; gated memory carries information across time steps. (c) Transformer: no known a-priori structure; permutation-invariant attention lets elements attend to each other and learn relational structure from data.

criteria.description: Correctly explains that summing h_{l-1} independent terms grows variance linearly with width.
Correctly explains that 1/h_{l-1} weight variance cancels this, preserving activation scale across depth.

solutions.fullSolution: A pre-activation sums h_{l-1} roughly-independent terms; variance of a sum of independent terms grows linearly with the number of terms. So without correction, Var{z} ~ h_{l-1}*v*Var{x}, meaning wider layers give systematically larger pre-activations regardless of learned structure. Choosing weight variance v=1/h_{l-1} cancels this factor, giving Var{z}~Var{x} regardless of width: activation scale is preserved across depth instead of compounding exponentially.

criteria.description: Correctly explains each dropout pattern as a distinct sub-network, exponentially many total.
Correctly explains why scaling by p at prediction time approximates the ensemble average.

solutions.fullSolution: Each dropout pattern defines a distinct sub-network sharing the same weights; exponentially many patterns exist, so training with dropout is like training an enormous weight-sharing ensemble. Ideally you'd average all their predictions at test time, infeasible explicitly. Scaling by p (keep-probability) approximates this: each unit was present a fraction p of the time on average during training, so scaling by p approximates the ensemble-averaged activation without enumerating the sub-networks.
